newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's 1977 cabinet mulled rejecting Quebec vote.
newsitem.headline: Canada's 1977 cabinet mulled rejecting Quebec vote.

text.p: Canada's federal cabinet 20 years ago discussed rejecting any Quebec referendum on separation and using military force in the French-speaking province, the Ottawa Citizen reported on Monday.
The disclosure, based on previously secret cabinet documents obtained under the Access to Information Act, raised an issue that few leaders since then would have dared to discuss openly.
The newspaper quoted Warren Allmand, then Indian Affairs minister, as saying in January 1977 that the government should declare it would reject a referendum.
"It was not for Quebec alone to decide whether Canada was to exist or not," the minutes quoted him as telling Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau's cabinet.
"Therefore, the government should say it would not accept any referendum that would separate the Maritimes (the Atlantic provinces) from the rest of Canada," he said.

The current prime minister, Jean Chretien, said in his re-election campaign in May that he would not accept a simple majority result in a Quebec referendum. But he has never suggested publicly that he would block a vote by, say, two-thirds or three-quarters of Quebec voters.
Separatists lost a referendum in 1980 by 60 to 40 percent and a second one in 1995 by only 50.6 to 49.4 percent.
The Citizen quoted Allmand as telling the cabinet: "The government should say that, as the federal authority, it would act (to defend the constitution)."

It quoted Allmand, now a human rights official, as saying in a current interview: "If somebody starts acting illegally or violently to violate the Constitution, then we have to enforce the law and use whatever is necessary to enforce the law, including the military."
Romeo LeBlanc, then minister of state for fisheries and now Canada's governor-general, spoke of the need for a "war-room mentality," the cabinet record said.
